source.body_text: In 1324, Mansa Musa of Mali crossed the Sahara with 60,000 people and so much gold that he crashed the precious metals market in Cairo. His journey was just one moment in a much larger story: the greatest pre-modern trading bloc in history. Journey across the Silk Road, the Indian Ocean dhow routes, and the trans-Saharan gold trade with Ibn Battuta as our guide. Topics: Silk Road, Indian Ocean Trade, Mansa Musa, Ibn Battuta, Trans-Saharan Trade, Amana (Trust) Series: Historical Islamic Economics (Part I) • Episode 5 of 6

x.single_post: In 1324, Mansa Musa of Mali crossed the Sahara with 60,000 people and so much gold that he crashed the precious metals market in Cairo. The parallels to today are hard to ignore.
thread: A medieval African king carried so much gold across the desert that he crashed Cairo's economy for a decade. The Federal Reserve prints money to manage inflation. Mansa Musa just walked into Egypt in 1324.
His caravan stretched for miles. 60,000 people crossed the Sahara together. When you control the world's gold supply, every step becomes monetary policy.
Ibn Battuta witnessed trade networks that spanned three continents. A merchant could send goods from Cordoba to Canton using nothing but reputation and paper.
The Silk Road, Indian Ocean routes, and trans-Saharan gold trade formed the world's first global economy. https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-5

linkedin.post: In 1324, Mansa Musa of Mali crossed the Sahara with 60,000 people and so much gold that he crashed Cairo's precious metals market for a decade. His journey reveals something profound about medieval trade networks. While Europe was still emerging from feudalism, Islamic merchants had already built the world's first truly global economy. The Silk Road, Indian Ocean dhow routes, and trans-Saharan gold trade created interconnected markets spanning three continents. Ibn Battuta could travel from Cordoba to Canton using nothing but reputation and paper instruments. Trust networks substituted for institutions we take for granted today. Modern economists study monetary policy through interest rates and quantitative easing. Medieval rulers practiced it by walking across deserts with caravans full of gold. Listen to the full episode: https://islamiceconomics.github.io/podcast.html#ep-5
linkedin.comment_prompt: What parallels do you see between medieval Islamic trade networks and today's global economy?

instagram.caption: In 1324, Mansa Musa of Mali crossed the Sahara with 60,000 people and so much gold that he crashed Cairo's economy for a decade. This wasn't just a pilgrimage. It was monetary policy in motion. While Europe was emerging from feudalism, Islamic merchants had built the world's first global economy. The Silk Road, Indian Ocean routes, and trans-Saharan gold trade connected three continents through networks of trust. Ibn Battuta witnessed merchants who could send goods from Spain to China using reputation alone. No banks, no international law, just shared principles and paper instruments. Modern central banks manage money supply through complex mechanisms. Mansa Musa did it by walking across the desert with more gold than Cairo had ever seen.
